Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: Rohan, a 35-year-old South Asian tax consultant, had always been driven by a sense of purpose. As a relief worker in a war zone, he had seen his fair share of devastation, but nothing could have prepared him for the trauma that would change his life forever. It started with the smell of smoke. The acrid scent would transport him back to the day when a makeshift hospital was bombed, killing dozens of civilians and leaving Rohan with survivor's guilt. Whenever he caught a whiff of smoke or fire, his mind would racingly replay the events of that fateful day. He would see himself trying to rescue people from the rubble, only to be forced back by the flames. The memories were fragmented, but one thing was certain – he had failed to protect others. As time passed, Rohan found himself avoiding anything that reminded him of the event. He stopped attending funerals or visiting cemeteries, afraid of being overwhelmed by grief. Even expressions of anger from others would send him into a panic, as if he were reliving the chaos and destruction of that day. He began to cover his face with his hands whenever these triggers arose, hoping to block out the sights and sounds. But avoiding the past only seemed to intensify Rohan's feelings of shame and isolation. When memories of the event surfaced, his body would involuntarily tense up, as if he were still trapped in that war-torn hospital. He couldn't concentrate on his work or sleep at night, haunted by the fear of being attacked again. The sounds of everyday life – a car backfiring or a door slamming shut – made him jump with a start. Rohan's negative appraisals about himself and the world began to take hold. He felt like he had failed as a human being, that his inability to protect others was a stain on his character. His sense of isolation deepened, as if he were the only one who truly understood what it meant to be shattered by trauma. As these feelings of shame and failure intensified, Rohan's maladaptive strategies became more entrenched. He started avoiding situations that might bring him joy or hope, afraid of being reminded of all that he had lost. His relationships with his loved ones began to suffer, as if he was perpetually stuck in a state of hypervigilance. Rohan's wife noticed the change in him and tried to reach out, but he pushed her away, fearing that she would see the shame and weakness he felt inside. He became withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings or meetings with friends. His work as a tax consultant began to suffer, as his concentration waned and his ability to focus dwindled. One day, while working late in his office, Rohan caught a whiff of smoke from a nearby fire drill. The familiar scent sent him tumbling back into the memories he had been trying so hard to avoid. His body tensed up, his mind racing with images of destruction and chaos. In that moment, Rohan realized that he needed help – not just to manage his symptoms but to confront the underlying fears and shame that had taken hold of his life. As he sat in his therapist's office, Rohan finally felt a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, he could learn to live with his trauma rather than being controlled by it. The thought was both exhilarating and terrifying – but for the first time in years, Rohan felt like he might be able to find a way out of the darkness that had consumed him.
